```{r}
# Importing packages
library(quantmod) # To access yfinance
library(bootUR) # For adf
library(forecast) # For ARIMA models, Acf and Pacf
library(vars) # For the VAR
library(zoo)
```

```{r}
# Data loading
jpm_data <- getSymbols('JPM', src='yahoo', from = "2005-01-01", to = "2025-12-31", auto.assign = FALSE)
```

We choose the period 1st of January 2005 to 31st of December 2025 to
obtain 20 years of daily data (approx 5040 (252 \*20) observations)
covering several significant structural breaks (2008 bank crisis, 2020
Covid-19).

# Data Exploration

```{r}
jpm_adj <- Ad(jpm_data) # Use adjusted close data as the price.
```

```{r}
plot(jpm_adj, main = "JPM Adjusted Close Price (2005-2025)", col = "navy", major.ticks = "years")
```

By observing the plot of the Adj-Close time series we can probably see
that it is non-stationary. It clearly has an upwards trend.

```{r}
crises <- list(
  "2008 Financial Crisis" = c(start = "2008-01-01", end = "2009-12-31"),
  "2020 COVID Shock"     = c(start = "2020-01-01", end = "2020-12-31")
)

for (name in names(crises)) {
  date_range <- paste(crises[[name]]["start"], crises[[name]]["end"], sep = "/")

  crisis_subset <- jpm_adj[date_range]
  
  print(plot(crisis_subset, 
       main = paste("JPM Stock Price:", name), 
       col = "darkred", 
       major.ticks = "months",
       grid.ticks.on = "months"))
}
```

For structural breaks, we notice a small dip during the 2008 financial
crisis. We can also find dips during the 2020 Covid-19 Pandemic.

# Unit Root Tests

We use the ADF test for the Pantula Principle. The Pantula principle
requires us to set a dmax, in this case it is sensible to choose dmax =
2. We will perform ADF tests for series differentiated dmax-times until
0 or until we fail to reject the null hypothesis of the ADF test that
the series is non-stationary (has unit root) and is I(d + 1).

```{r}
jpm_price <- na.omit(jpm_adj)
```

```{r}
diff2_jpm <- diff(jpm_price, differences = 2)[-c(1, 2)]
adf_d2 <- boot_adf(diff2_jpm, deterministics = "none")
adf_d2
```

For d = 2, we reject the null-hypothesis, thus the 2-times
differentiated series is stationary.

```{r}
diff1_jpm <- diff(jpm_price, differences = 1)[-1]
adf_d1 <- boot_adf(diff1_jpm, deterministics = "intercept")
adf_d1
```

We continue to d = 1, we also reject the H0, and thus, the 1-time
differentiated series is stationary.

```{r}
adf_d0 <- boot_adf(jpm_price, deterministics = "trend")
adf_d0
```

Finally, for d = 0, we fail to reject the H0 and thus the adjusted close
series is non-stationary because it has a unit root.

From this we can conclude that the series is I(1).

```{r}
plot(diff1_jpm, col = "darkblue")
```

# ARIMA Models for the Price Series

```{r}
jpm_price <- na.omit(jpm_adj)

diff_jpm <- diff(jpm_price)[-1]
```

We know the price series is I(1) se we now use the first differences
series

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
Acf(diff_jpm, main = "ACF of First Differences (ΔY_t)")
Pacf(diff_jpm, main = "PACF of First Differences (ΔY_t)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
fit_arima111 <- Arima(jpm_price, order = c(1, 1, 1), include.drift = TRUE)
fit_arima212 <- Arima(jpm_price, order = c(2, 1, 2), include.drift = TRUE)
fit_arima010 <- Arima(jpm_price, order = c(0, 1, 0), include.drift = TRUE)
```

Standard R functions like stats::arima() only allow a drift term when d
= 0. The forecast::Arima() allows inclusion of a constant term c when we
differentiatie once. And since we know our series is I(1) we need to use
the forecast package.

```{r}
aicc_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift", "ARIMA(1,1,1) with drift", "ARIMA(2,1,2) with drift"),
  AICc  = c(fit_arima010$aicc, fit_arima111$aicc, fit_arima212$aicc)
)
print(aicc_table)
```

We choose as the best model the one with the lowest AICc, which is
ARIMA(2, 1, 2).

```{r}
auto_fit <- auto.arima(
  jpm_price,
  d = 1,                   # We know its I(1)
  max.p = 5,               # Set max search bounds
  max.q = 5, 
  stepwise = TRUE,         # Uses Hyndman-Khandakar stepwise algorithm
  approximation = FALSE,
  ic = "aicc"              # Selects model based on Corrected AIC
)

summary(auto_fit)
```

An ARIMA(4, 1, 2) is selected as the optimal model, it achieves an AICc
of 19785.51, which is lower than the one we achieved using our
hard-coded models.

# From prices to Returns

We will use log-returns, the reasons for this decision are: -
Log-returns are linearly additive over time, while simple returns must
be compounded through multiplication. - When price series are long, raw
prices increase rapidly, simple returns can suffer from big variance
differences, while log returns scale variance and return more stationary
variance properties.

```{r}
jpm_returns <- na.omit(diff(log(jpm_adj)))

plot(jpm_returns, main = "JPM Daily Log Returns", ylab = "Log Return")
```

The series looks stationary from visual examination

```{r}
boot_adf(jpm_returns, deterministics = "intercept")
```

We run the ADF test only with intercept because the mean of the log
returns series is not exactly zero, since stock prices have an upwards
trend. Using the ADF test we can reject the null hypothesis that the
series has a unit root, and thus determine that our log returns are a
stationary time series.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
Acf(jpm_returns, main = "ACF of log-returns")
Pacf(jpm_returns, main = "PACF of log-returns")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
auto_fit <- auto.arima(
  jpm_returns,
  d = 0,                   # We know log returns are stationary
  max.p = 5,               # Set max search bounds
  max.q = 5, 
  stepwise = TRUE,
  approximation = FALSE,
  ic = "aicc"              # Selects model based on Corrected AIC
)

summary(auto_fit)
```

From the auto.arima function we select the ARIMA(3, 0, 2).

# GARCH models: Modeling volatility

The ARIMA models we fit above model the conditional mean of the returns,
assuming the errors are homoskedastic, meaning they have a constant
variance. But financial returns are well known for their volatility
clustering: large price changes tend to be followed by more large price
changes, and small changes tend to be followed by small changes.This
means the variance of the errors is not constant over time, but it is
itsef autocorrelated. Even when the returns themselves are uncorrelated.

(G)ARCH models (Bollershev, 1986) shift the focus from modeling the
conditional mean to modelling the conditional variance.

The GARCH(1,1):

$$r_t = \mu_t + \epsilon_t, \qquad \epsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1)$$
$$\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1\epsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2$$
Today's conditional variance $\sigma_t^2$ depends on a constant
$\omega$, yesterday's shock squared $\epsilon_{t-1}^2$, and yesterday's
conditional variance $\sigma_{t-1}^2$. This is very similar compared to
the ARMA model, but then applied to the squared residuals (variance)
instead of the level of the series (mean).

Stylized facts GARCH captures and ARIMA can't: (i)Volatility clustering
(described above) (ii)Heteroskedasticity: Variance can change over time,
no longer constant is in ARIMA models. (iii)Fat tails: Because of the
adjusted variance at every time step, you are not forced to use a normal
distribution for the error terms.Under a normal distribution, the
probability of an extreme event (market crash) is calculated as really
small. In real life, these extreme outliers happen much more frequently
than a normal distribution predicts. (iv)Mean reverting volatility:
After a shock, volatility eventually settles back toward a long-run
average level. At the rate $alpha_1$ + $beta_1$.

# Checking for ARCH effects:

Before we implement the GARCH model, we first check whether there is
statistical evidence for ARCH. We do this by looking at the
autocorrelation of the squared returns. If returns themselves are close
to white noise, but their squares are autocorrelated, there is direct
evidence of volatility clustering.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
Acf(jpm_returns^2, main = "ACF of squared log-returns")

Pacf(jpm_returns^2, main= "PACF of squared log-returns")
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

```{r}
#ARCH-LM test (formal test for ARCH effects)
library(FinTS)
ArchTest(jpm_returns, lags = 12)
```

We reject the null hypothesis, so a GARCH model is necessary.

# Estimating a GARCH(1,1) model

We use the rugarch package, the standard package for GARCH models. This
is because it supports many variance specifications and multiple error
distributions(normal, Student-t, skewed-t, etc).

```{r}
#Garch(1,1) with a Student-t distribution for the #standardized errors. We do this to accomodate for the #fat tails observed in daily equity returns.
#The mean equation is specified as ARMA(3,2), matching #the auto.arima selection for the return series above.
library(rugarch)
spec_garch11 <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(3,2), include.mean = TRUE),
distribution.model = "std"
)
fit_garch11 <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_garch11, data = jpm_returns)
fit_garch11
```

# Interpreting the estimated model

```{r}
coef(fit_garch11)
```

Recall
that:$$\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha_1\epsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1\sigma_{t-1}^2$$
We see the small constant omega, the floor level of the variance without
any shocks. $\alpha1 = 0.099$ ,so moderate reaction to new shocks: about
10% of yesterday's squared shock feeds into today's variance.
$\beta1 = 0.893$ , so this means today's variance carries forward
roughly 89% of yesterday's conditional variance.
$\alpha1 + \beta1 = 0.9915$ , which is very close to 1. This means the
model implies stationary, but only weakly stationary. The shocks to
volatility die out only very slowly. Shape =4.99, this is the estimated
degrees of freedom of the Student-t distribution. A value this low is
strong evidence of fat tails: JPM's daily returns show substantially
more extreme outcome probability then a normal distribution would
predict.

```{r}
plot(fit_garch11, which = 3)
```

# Diagnostics

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
Acf(residuals(fit_garch11, standardize = TRUE), main = "ACF of standardized residuals")
Acf(residuals(fit_garch11, standardize = TRUE)^2, main = "ACF of squared standardized residuals")
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

```{r}
infocriteria(fit_garch11)
```

We have negative numbers here. This is because information criteria are
built from log-likelihood. These log-likelihood uses returns, which are
in our case small numbers with small variance. Making the information
criteria negative. Still holds: the lower the information criteria, the
better.

# Comparing the information criteria of the student-t distribution to the normal distribution.

```{r}
spec_norm <- ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(3,2), include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = "norm"
)
fit_norm <- ugarchfit(spec = spec_norm, data = jpm_returns)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("GARCH(1,1), Student-t", "GARCH(1,1), Normal"),
  AIC = c(infocriteria(fit_garch11)[1], infocriteria(fit_norm)[1]),
  BIC = c(infocriteria(fit_garch11)[2], infocriteria(fit_norm)[2])
)
print(comparison)
```

We see that the difference is 0.087 for AIC and 0.086 for BIC. Since the
lower the better, and this gap is far from negligible, this is clear
evidence that the Student-t distribution fits the JPM returns better
than the normal distribution. This confirms our choice of the student-t
distribution.

# HAR MODEL

# Bridging the Data Gap: Realized Range

We would like intraday data (5min/15min/1h), since yahoo finance can´t
provide that we use the Parkinson’s Realized Range estimator which is:
$$RR_t = \frac{(\ln(H_t) - \ln(L_t))^2}{4 \ln(2)}$$ Basically we need
The daily High price and the daily Low price, instead of adjusted close.

```{r}
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)
```

Model formulation is as follows:
$$RR_t = \beta_0 + \beta_d RR_{t-1} + \beta_w RR_{t-1}^{(w)} + \beta_m RR_{t-1}^{(m)} + \varepsilon_t$$

```{r}
RR <- ((log(Hi(jpm_data)) - log(Lo(jpm_data)))^2) / (4 * log(2))
colnames(RR) <- "RR"

RR_d <- Lag(RR, 1)
RR_w <- Lag(rollmean(RR, k = 5, fill = NA, align = "right"), 1)
RR_m <- Lag(rollmean(RR, k = 22, fill = NA, align = "right"), 1)

har_range_data <- na.omit(merge(RR, RR_d, RR_w, RR_m))
colnames(har_range_data) <- c("RR", "RR_d", "RR_w", "RR_m")

har_range_model <- lm(RR ~ RR_d + RR_w + RR_m, data = har_range_data)

coeftest(har_range_model, vcov = NeweyWest(har_range_model, lag = 5))
```

We use Newey-West heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent
(HAC) standard errors because standard OLS standard errors are biased
here since financial volatility series exhibit strong autocorrelation
and conditional heteroskedasticity.

From the coefficient test we can see that the lagged daily RR is
significant, together with the monthly RR. The weekly RR is not
significant when daily RR is taken into account. I need to economically
justify this!

```{r}
res <- residuals(har_range_model)
Acf(res, main = "ACF of Residuals")
plot(har_range_model, which = 3)
```

```{r}
plot(RR, 
     main = "JPM - Daily Realized Range Volatility (2005-2025)",
     ylab = "Realized Range (RR)",
     xlab = "Date",
     col = "darkred",
     lwd = 1,
     major.ticks = "years",
     grid.ticks.on = "years",
     grid.col = "lightgray")

# Adding a visual highlight for major economic stress periods
addEventLines(
  events = xts(c("2008 Crisis", "2020 COVID"), 
               as.Date(c("2008-09-15", "2020-03-11"))),
  col = "navy", 
  srt = 90, 
  pos = 2
)
```

```{r}
# Extract fitted values from the HAR model
rr_fitted <- xts(fitted(har_range_model), order.by = index(har_range_data))

# Merge actual RR and fitted values into an xts object
# Note: fitted values start after the initial NA alignment from lagging
rr_comparison <- merge(har_range_data$RR, rr_fitted)
colnames(rr_comparison) <- c("Actual_RR", "Predicted_RR")

# 1. Plot ONLY the actual series first (Background layer: muted gray line)
plot(rr_comparison$Actual_RR, 
     main = "Actual vs Fitted HAR Realized Range",
     col = "gray70",                # Light gray puts actual data in the background
     lwd = 1,
     major.ticks = "years",
     grid.ticks.on = "years",
     ylab = "Realized Range")

# 2. Draw the predicted series on TOP (Foreground layer: bold red line)
lines(rr_comparison$Predicted_RR, 
      col = "firebrick",            # Bright red brings predicted values to the front
      lwd = 1.3)

# 3. Add the legend
addLegend(legend.loc = "topright", 
          legend.names = c("Actual RR", "Predicted RR (HAR)"), 
          col = c("gray70", "firebrick"), 
          lty = c(1, 1), 
          lwd = c(1, 1.3),
          bg = "white")
```

# Bridging the Data Gap: Monthly Realized Variance from Daily Data

Following the previous section, another option in case intraday data is
not available is to still try to model volatility but raising the
aggregation level to monthly. This is done by:
$$RV_{m} = \sum_{i \in \text{month}} r_{i}^2$$ The formulated model is:
$$RV_{m} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 RV_{m-1} + \beta_3 RV_{m-1}^{(3)} + \beta_{12} RV_{m-1}^{(12)} + \varepsilon_m$$

```{r}
rv_monthly <- apply.monthly(jpm_returns, function(x) sum(x^2, na.rm = TRUE))
colnames(rv_monthly) <- "RV_m"

RV_m1  <- Lag(rv_monthly, 1)
RV_m3  <- Lag(rollmean(rv_monthly, k = 3, fill = NA, align = "right"), 1)
RV_m12 <- Lag(rollmean(rv_monthly, k = 12, fill = NA, align = "right"), 1)

# 4. Combine and remove NA values generated by rolling/lagging
har_monthly_data <- na.omit(merge(rv_monthly, RV_m1, RV_m3, RV_m12))
colnames(har_monthly_data) <- c("RV_m", "RV_m1", "RV_m3", "RV_m12")

# 5. Estimate the Monthly HAR model
har_monthly_model <- lm(RV_m ~ RV_m1 + RV_m3 + RV_m12, data = har_monthly_data)

# 6. Output summary with robust standard errors
coeftest(har_monthly_model, vcov = NeweyWest(har_monthly_model))
```

From the coefficient test we can see that the only significant
coefficient is the medium term volatility (quarterly). This makes us
think that the primary market predictor for a stock like JPM is the
intermediate market memory.

Issue: Aggregartion bias: Aggregating daily data to monthly realized
variance smooths out single-month noise, shifting structural persistence
toward quarterly trends.

# A Multivariate Extension: Modeling Spillovers.

```{r}
# 1. Collect data for JPM, BAC, and MSFT (2005-2025)
tickers <- c("JPM", "BAC", "MSFT")
multi_data <- new.env()
getSymbols(tickers, src = "yahoo", from = "2005-01-01", to = "2025-12-31", env = multi_data)

# 2. Compute Daily Realized Range (RR) for each stock
calc_rr <- function(xts_obj) {
  rr <- ((log(Hi(xts_obj)) - log(Lo(xts_obj)))^2) / (4 * log(2))
  rr[rr <= 0] <- NA
  colnames(rr) <- "RR"
  return(rr)
}

rr_jpm <- calc_rr(multi_data$JPM)
rr_bac <- calc_rr(multi_data$BAC)
rr_msft <- calc_rr(multi_data$MSFT)

# 3. Construct HAR components (Daily, Weekly (5-day rolling), Monthly (22-day rolling))
make_har_features <- function(rr_series) {
  y <- log(rr_series)
  d <- stats::lag(log(rr_series), 1)
  w <- stats::lag(log(rollmean(rr_series, k = 5, fill = NA, align = "right")), 1)
  m <- stats::lag(log(rollmean(rr_series, k = 22, fill = NA, align = "right")), 1)
  res <- na.omit(merge(y, d, w, m))
  colnames(res) <- c("RR", "RR_d", "RR_w", "RR_m")
  return(res)
}

# 4. Apply your make_har_features function to each asset's Realized Range series
har_jpm <- make_har_features(rr_jpm)
har_bac <- make_har_features(rr_bac)
har_msft <- make_har_features(rr_msft)
colnames(har_jpm) <- paste0("JPM_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))
colnames(har_bac) <- paste0("BAC_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))
colnames(har_msft) <- paste0("MSFT_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))

m_har_data <- na.omit(merge(har_jpm, har_bac, har_msft))

# --- Equation 1: JPM M-HAR Model ---
mhar_jpm_model <- lm(JPM_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + 
                              BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + 
                              MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, 
                     data = m_har_data)

# --- Equation 2: BAC M-HAR Model ---
mhar_bac_model <- lm(BAC_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + 
                              BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + 
                              MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, 
                     data = m_har_data)

# --- Equation 3: MSFT M-HAR Model ---
mhar_msft_model <- lm(MSFT_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + 
                               BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + 
                               MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, 
                      data = m_har_data)
```

```{r}
cat("\n=== JPM M-HAR Spillovers ===\n")
print(coeftest(mhar_jpm_model, vcov = NeweyWest(mhar_jpm_model, lag = 5)))

cat("\n=== BAC M-HAR Spillovers ===\n")
print(coeftest(mhar_bac_model, vcov = NeweyWest(mhar_bac_model, lag = 5)))

cat("\n=== MSFT M-HAR Spillovers ===\n")
print(coeftest(mhar_msft_model, vcov = NeweyWest(mhar_msft_model, lag = 5)))
```

We see that the weekly components are the most significant ones.

We see some significance of JPM to BAC and MSFT to JPM

```{r}
spill_test <- function(model, from) {
  h <- paste0(from, c("_d", "_w", "_m"))s
  b <- coef(model)[h]                      #Their estimates
  V <- NeweyWest(model, lag = 5)[h,h]      #Newey-West covariance matrix
  W <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(V) %*% b) #Wald statistic
  pchisq(W, df = length(h), lower.tail = FALSE) #p-value from chi-squared(3)
}
full_tests <- c(
  "JPM -> BAC" = spill_test(mhar_bac_model, "JPM"),
  "JPM -> MSFT" = spill_test(mhar_msft_model, "JPM"),
  "BAC -> JPM" = spill_test(mhar_jpm_model, "BAC"),
  "BAC -> MSFT" = spill_test(mhar_msft_model, "BAC"),
  "MSFT -> JPM" = spill_test(mhar_jpm_model, "MSFT"),
  "MSFT -> BAC" = spill_test(mhar_bac_model, "MSFT")
)
```

# Subsample Analysis: Crisis versus Non-crisis Periods.

```{r}
# 1. Re-generate HAR features for the entire multi-system first
har_jpm <- make_har_features(rr_jpm)
har_bac <- make_har_features(rr_bac)
har_msft <- make_har_features(rr_msft)

colnames(har_jpm) <- paste0("JPM_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))
colnames(har_bac) <- paste0("BAC_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))
colnames(har_msft) <- paste0("MSFT_", c("RR", "d", "w", "m"))

m_har_full <- na.omit(merge(har_jpm, har_bac, har_msft))

# 2. Split the M-HAR dataset into Crisis and Non-Crisis subsets using window()
crisis_data_1 <- window(m_har_full, start = "2008-01-01", end = "2009-12-31")
crisis_data_2 <- window(m_har_full, start = "2020-01-01", end = "2020-12-31")
m_har_crisis <- rbind(crisis_data_1, crisis_data_2)

m_har_noncrisis <- window(m_har_full, start = "2011-01-01", end = "2019-12-31")

# 3. Estimate M-HAR Equations for the CRISIS Period (Including MSFT)
cat("\n================ CRISIS PERIOD M-HAR (2008 & 2020) ================\n")
crisis_jpm <- lm(JPM_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_crisis)
crisis_bac <- lm(BAC_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_crisis)
crisis_msft <- lm(MSFT_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_crisis)

print("--- JPM Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(crisis_jpm, vcov = NeweyWest(crisis_jpm, lag = 5)))

print("--- BAC Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(crisis_bac, vcov = NeweyWest(crisis_bac, lag = 5)))

print("--- MSFT Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(crisis_msft, vcov = NeweyWest(crisis_msft, lag = 5)))

crisis_tests <- c(
  "JPM -> BAC" = spill_test(crisis_bac, "JPM"),
  "JPM -> MSFT" = spill_test(crisis_msft, "JPM"),
  "BAC -> JPM" = spill_test(crisis_jpm, "BAC"),
  "BAC -> MSFT" = spill_test(crisis_msft, "BAC"),
  "MSFT -> JPM" = spill_test(crisis_jpm, "MSFT"),
  "MSFT -> BAC" = spill_test(crisis_bac, "MSFT")
  )


# 4. Estimate M-HAR Equations for the NON-CRISIS Period (Including MSFT)
cat("\n================ NON-CRISIS PERIOD M-HAR (2011-2019) ================\n")
noncrisis_jpm <- lm(JPM_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_noncrisis)
noncrisis_bac <- lm(BAC_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_noncrisis)
noncrisis_msft <- lm(MSFT_RR ~ JPM_d + JPM_w + JPM_m + BAC_d + BAC_w + BAC_m + MSFT_d + MSFT_w + MSFT_m, data = m_har_noncrisis)

print("--- JPM Non-Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(noncrisis_jpm, vcov = NeweyWest(noncrisis_jpm, lag = 5)))

print("--- BAC Non-Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(noncrisis_bac, vcov = NeweyWest(noncrisis_bac, lag = 5)))

print("--- MSFT Non-Crisis Spillovers ---")
print(coeftest(noncrisis_msft, vcov = NeweyWest(noncrisis_msft, lag = 5)))

noncrisis_tests <- c(
  "JPM -> BAC" = spill_test(noncrisis_bac, "JPM"),
  "JPM -> MSFT" = spill_test(noncrisis_msft, "JPM"),
  "BAC -> JPM" = spill_test(noncrisis_jpm, "BAC"),
  "BAC -> MSFT" = spill_test(noncrisis_msft, "BAC"),
  "MSFT -> JPM" = spill_test(noncrisis_jpm, "MSFT"),
  "MSFT -> BAC" = spill_test(noncrisis_bac, "MSFT")
  )
spill_table <- round(cbind(Full = full_tests, Crisis = crisis_tests, NonCrisis = noncrisis_tests), 4)
print(spill_table)
```
```{r}
cor(cbind(JPM = resid(crisis_jpm), BAC = resid(crisis_bac), MSFT = resid(crisis_msft)))
cor(cbind(JPM = resid(noncrisis_jpm), BAC = resid(noncrisis_bac), MSFT = resid(noncrisis_msft)))
```
Across both regimes we see the weekly dominance again.

During crises MSFT affects JPM, non crises BAC affects JPM.

The comparison reveals regime-dependent spillover pathways: during
structural crises, high-frequency banking shocks (JPM $\rightarrow$ BAC)
and broad market panic (MSFT $\rightarrow$ JPM) intensify, whereas
calmer periods exhibit more localized or cross-sector baseline
interactions.
